verses.35:7: that is, forty-eight altogether, with their outlying lands.
verses.35:8: And as for the cities themselves that will be given from the possessions of the sons of Israel: from those who have more, more will be taken, and from those who have less, fewer; each one will give towns to the Levites according to the measure of his inheritance."
verses.35:10: "Speak to the sons of Israel, and you will say to them: 'When you have crossed the Jordan into the land of Canaan,
verses.35:11: designate which cities ought to be for the protection of fugitives who have shed blood unintentionally,
verses.35:12: in which, when the fugitive is there, the kinsman of the one killed will not be able to kill him until he stands in the sight of the multitude and his case is judged.
verses.35:13: Now of those very cities that are set apart for the refuge of fugitives,
verses.35:14: three will be across the Jordan and three in the land of Canaan,
verses.35:15: both for the sons of Israel and for strangers and sojourners, so that the one who has shed blood unintentionally may flee to them.
verses.35:16: If anyone strikes with iron, and the one who was struck dies, he will be guilty of murder, and he himself will die.
verses.35:17: If he throws a stone, and the one struck falls dead, he will be punished in the same way.
verses.35:18: If one struck with wood perishes, he will be avenged by the blood of the striker.
verses.35:19: The close relative of the one killed will put the murderer to death; as soon as he seizes him, he will put him to death.
verses.35:20: If anyone pushes a person out of hatred, or throws anything at him from ambush,
verses.35:21: or, being an enemy, strikes him with his hand, and that one dies, the striker will be guilty of murder; the kinsman of the one killed, as soon as he finds him, will execute him.
verses.35:22: But if by chance, and without hatred
verses.35:23: and hostilities, he has done any of these things,
verses.35:24: and this has been proven in the hearing of the people, and the inquiry has been examined between the striker and the close relative of the blood,
verses.35:25: the innocent one will be freed from the hand of the avenger, and he will be brought back by verdict into the city to which he had fled, and he will remain there until the high priest, who was anointed with the holy oil, dies.
verses.35:26: If the killer outside the borders of the cities that have been assigned to exiles
verses.35:27: is found and struck by the one who is the avenger of blood, the one who kills him will be without guilt.
verses.35:28: For the fugitive ought to have stayed in the city until the death of the high priest. But after he has died, the killer will return to his own land.
verses.35:29: These things will be perpetual and established by law in all your dwellings.
verses.35:30: A murderer will be punished under witnesses; on the testimony of one person, no one will be condemned.
verses.35:31: You will not accept a payment from one who is guilty of blood; he himself also will die immediately.
verses.35:32: Exiles and fugitives will by no means be able to return to their own cities before the death of the high priest,
verses.35:33: so that you do not pollute the land of your dwelling, which is stained by the blood of the innocent; nor can it be expiated in any other way except through the blood of the one who shed the blood of another.
verses.35:34: And thus your possession will be cleansed while I dwell with you. For I am the Lord, who dwell among the sons of Israel.'"
verses.36:1: Now the chiefs of the families of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the lineage of the sons of Joseph, also came forward; and they spoke to Moses before the chiefs of Israel and said,
verses.36:2: "The Lord commanded you, our lord, to divide the land by lot to the sons of Israel, and to give to the daughters of Zelophehad our brother the possession due to their father;
verses.36:3: and if men of another tribe take them as wives, their possession will follow, and, transferred to another tribe, it will be deducted from our inheritance.
verses.36:4: And so it will happen that when the Jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year of release, arrives, the distribution of the lots will be confused, and the possession of some will pass over to others."
verses.36:5: Moses answered the sons of Israel, and at the Lord's command he said, "The tribe of the sons of Joseph has spoken rightly.
verses.36:6: And this law concerning the daughters of Zelophehad has been proclaimed by the Lord: let them marry whomever they wish, provided they marry only men of their own tribe,
verses.36:7: so that the possession of the sons of Israel may not be mingled from tribe to tribe. For all men will take wives from their own tribe and clan,
verses.36:8: and all women will take husbands from the same tribe, so that the inheritance may remain in the families,
verses.36:9: and the tribes may not be mingled with one another, but may remain
verses.36:10: just as they were separated by the Lord." And the daughters of Zelophehad did as had been commanded,
verses.36:11: and Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah married the sons of their father's brother
verses.36:12: from the family of Manasseh, who was the son of Joseph; and the possession that had been assigned to them remained in the tribe and family of their father.
verses.36:13: These are the commands and judgments that the Lord commanded through the hand of Moses to the sons of Israel, in the plains of Moab by the Jordan, opposite Jericho.

notes.1:1: The Vulgate reads tabernaculo foederis ("tabernacle of the covenant"), whereas the Hebrew text has "tent of meeting."
notes.1:3: The Vulgate reads virorum fortium ("strong men"), where the Hebrew text reads "everyone able to go out to war."
notes.1:11: The Vulgate reads Gedeonis ("Gideon"), declining the patronymic as a form of Gideon, whereas the Hebrew text has "Gideoni."
notes.1:24: Native Vulgate Numbers 1:24-37 place Gad first (1:24-25), followed by Judah (1:26-27), Issachar (1:28-29), Zebulun (1:30-31), Ephraim (1:32-33), Manasseh (1:34-35), and Benjamin (1:36-37), mapping to Saints.Bible 1:36-37 and 1:24-35 respectively.
notes.1:50: The Vulgate specifies quidquid ad caeremonias pertinet ("whatever pertains to the ceremonies"), whereas the Hebrew text reads more generally "all that belongs to it."
notes.2:2: The Vulgate calls the sanctuary "tabernaculum foederis" (tabernacle of the covenant) here and "tabernaculum testimonii" (tabernacle of the testimony) in 2:17, where the Hebrew has "tent of meeting" in both verses.
notes.2:5: Within the Lord's instructions (2:2-31), the Vulgate alternates between future tense for the camp layout and order of march (2:2-3, 9-10, 16-18, 24, 31) and past tense for several tribal encampments and leaders (2:5, 7, 12, 14, 18, 25, 27), reflecting the already completed organization and census of chapter 1.
notes.2:14: The Vulgate reads "Duel" (Deuel), matching Numbers 1:14, 7:42, and 10:20, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Reuel" here.
notes.2:17: Distinctively, the Vulgate describes the tabernacle of the testimony being lifted up through the services of the Levites and taken down just as it will be erected, whereas the Hebrew describes the tent of meeting setting out with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps, setting out just as they camp.
notes.2:22: The Vulgate reads "Gedeonis" (genitive of "Gedeon", i.e., Gideon), whereas the Hebrew text names Abidan's father "Gideoni".
notes.3:10: The Vulgate specifies that the outsider approaches "to minister" (ad ministrandum), a detail not explicit in the Hebrew text. Native Vulgate 3:9-10 divide the sentence after "as a gift."
notes.3:25: The Vulgate renders Hebrew ohel mo'ed ("tent of meeting") here and in 3:38 as tabernaculum foederis ("tabernacle of the covenant")—and in 3:26 as tectum foederis ("shelter of the covenant")—whereas in 3:7 it renders the same Hebrew phrase as tabernaculum testimonii ("tabernacle of the testimony").
notes.3:38: The Vulgate uniquely reads in medio filiorum Israel ("in the midst of the sons of Israel"), whereas the Hebrew text reads "for the charge/obligation of the sons of Israel."
notes.3:47: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew weight unit gerah with the Greek-derived term obolos ("obols"), and refers to the sanctuary standard as mensuram sanctuarii ("measure of the sanctuary") here and pondus sanctuarii ("weight of the sanctuary") in 3:50.
notes.3:49: The Vulgate reads et quos redemerant a Levitis ("and whom they had redeemed from the Levites"), whereas the Hebrew text speaks of those over and above "those redeemed by the Levites."
notes.4:4: The Clementine Vulgate links verses 4 and 5 syntactically, making "the tabernacle of the covenant and the Holy of Holies" (tabernaculum foederis, et Sanctum sanctorum) the direct object of "shall enter" (ingredientur), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text ends verse 4 with "the most holy things."
notes.4:6: The Vulgate renders the obscure Hebrew hide term (tachash) by color as "violet skins" (janthinarum pellium; also in vv. 8, 10, 11, 12, 14, and 25), keeping it distinct from hyacinthinus ("blue") and purpureus ("purple").
notes.4:14: The Vulgate lists five altar implements (fire receptacles, small forks, three-pronged forks, hooks, and shovels) and specifies "All the vessels of the altar" (Cuncta vasa altaris), whereas the Hebrew text lists four implements and reads simply "upon it."
notes.4:20: "Others shall not look with any curiosity" translates the distinctly Vulgate phrasing Alii nulla curiositate videant; the Hebrew Masoretic Text forbids going in to see the holy things even for a moment (or as they are covered).
notes.4:32: The Vulgate reads "by number" (ad numerum) for receiving the equipment, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "by name."
notes.5:3: The Vulgate reads cum habitaverint vobiscum ("while they dwell with you"), referring to those expelled, whereas the Hebrew text reads "in the midst of which I dwell."
notes.5:15: The Vulgate specifies decimam partem sati ("a tenth part of a seah," a dry measure equal to one-third of an ephah), whereas the Hebrew text specifies a tenth of an ephah.
notes.5:21: The Vulgate reads in populo suo ("among His people") and vividly renders the curse as the thigh rotting and the swelling womb bursting apart, differing from the Hebrew ("among your people"; thigh wasting away and belly swelling).
notes.5:26: The Vulgate qualifying clause ita dumtaxat ut prius ("provided, however, that first," closing 5:25) clarifies that the handful of the sacrifice is burned before the woman drinks the bitter waters.
notes.6:4: The Vulgate reads ab uva passa usque ad acinum ("from the raisin even to the seed"), whereas the Hebrew text reads "from the seeds even to the skin."
notes.6:9: The Vulgate prescribes shaving immediately on that day of purification and again on the seventh (illico ... et rursum septima), whereas the Hebrew text describes a single shaving on the seventh day.
notes.6:10: The Vulgate uniquely reads in introitu foederis testimonii ("at the entrance of the covenant of the testimony") where the Hebrew text has "at the entrance of the tent of meeting."
notes.6:23: Native Vulgate Numbers 6:23-27 place the closing promise (6:27, 'And they shall invoke My name...') separately after the Aaronic blessing in 6:24-26, matching the Hebrew order (whereas Saints.Bible Septuagint-aligned display places this clause before the blessing in 6:23).
notes.6:25: In verses 25-26, the Vulgate distinctively renders the blessing with Ostendat ("show") and misereatur ("have mercy on") in verse 25, and Convertat ("turn") in verse 26, where the Hebrew reads "make shine," "be gracious to," and "lift up."
notes.6:27: Native Vulgate Numbers 6:27 stands separately after the blessing (6:24-26) and renders Hebrew "put My name" as "invoke My name" (Invocabuntque nomen meum).
notes.7:1: Vulgate complevit ... et erexit ("completed ... and erected") uses two coordinate finite verbs where the Hebrew reads "finished setting up."
notes.7:13: Throughout this chapter, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew grain offering (minchah) simply as sacrificium ("sacrifice") and the standard weight as pondus sanctuarii ("weight of the sanctuary") rather than "shekel of the sanctuary."
notes.7:14: Vulgate mortariolum ("small mortar") translates Hebrew kaph ("pan" or "ladle"); here it is described as ex decem siclis aureis ("made of ten gold shekels"), while later verses shift to habens ("of ten shekels," v. 20) and appendens ("weighing ten shekels," vv. 26, 32, 38, 44).
notes.7:60: Latin Gedeonis is the genitive of Gedeon ("Gideon"), whereas the Hebrew reads Gid'oni ("Gideoni"); the same form recurs in 7:65.
notes.7:87: Vulgate libamenta ("drink offerings" or "libations") differs from the Hebrew, which reads minchah ("grain offering").
notes.7:89: Vulgate tabernaculum foederis ("tabernacle of the covenant") renders Hebrew "tent of meeting," and ut consuleret oraculum ("to consult the oracle") stands where the Hebrew reads "to speak with Him."
notes.8:2: The Vulgate expands the brief Hebrew directive by explicitly specifying the lampstand's placement on the south side and its north-facing orientation toward the table of the loaves of presentation (panum propositionis), in line with Exodus 26:35.
notes.8:4: The Vulgate describes the lampstand as "both the central shaft and all that sprang forth from both sides of the branches" (tam medius stipes, quam cuncta quæ ex utroque calamorum latere nascebantur), where the Hebrew reads "from its base to its flowers."
notes.8:8: Latin libamentum (literally "libation" or "offering") is used here by the Vulgate for the accompanying grain offering, defined in apposition as fine flour mixed with oil.
notes.8:9: Throughout this chapter, the Vulgate renders Hebrew ohel mo'ed ("tent of meeting") as tabernaculum fœderis, "tabernacle of the covenant."
notes.8:12: Here (ut depreceris pro eis) and in verses 19 and 21 (orent / oravit), the Vulgate uses verbs of intercession and prayer where the Hebrew specifies making atonement; likewise, in verse 21 elevavit ("lifted up") renders the Hebrew wave-offering ritual.
notes.9:5: The Vulgate reads in monte Sinai ("on Mount Sinai"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Septuagint read "in the wilderness of Sinai" (as in 9:1).
notes.9:6: Latin super anima hominis ("on account of the soul of a person," also in 9:7 and 9:10) literally reproduces the Hebrew idiom (le-nefesh adam) for ritual impurity contracted through contact with a human corpse.
notes.9:10: The Vulgate reads in gente vestra ("in your nation"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to you or to your generations."
notes.9:11: Latin lactucis agrestibus specifically identifies the Passover bitter herbs (Hebrew merorim) as "wild lettuce," consistent with the Vulgate of Exodus 12:8.
notes.9:19: The Vulgate connects verses 19 and 20 into a single sentence ("did not set out for as many days as the cloud was over the tabernacle"), whereas the Hebrew begins a new clause in verse 20; in verses 19 and 23, erant in excubiis Domini uses a Latin military phrase for keeping watch.
notes.10:3: Latin tabernaculi foederis ("tabernacle of the covenant") is the Vulgate's consistent rendering here, in 10:11, and in 11:16, where the Hebrew has "tent of meeting" (10:3, 11:16) or "tabernacle of the testimony" (10:11).
notes.10:4: Vulgate Si semel clangueris ("If you blow once") renders the Hebrew expression adverbially as a single blast rather than as blowing only one of the two trumpets.
notes.10:6: Latin ululatus and ululare (literally "wailing" or "ululating," also in 10:7 and 10:9) render the broken, ringing alarm blast of the trumpets (Hebrew teruah).
notes.10:21: The Vulgate states that the tabernacle continued to be carried until they reached the place of setting it up, whereas the Hebrew states that the tabernacle was erected before the Kohathites arrived.
notes.10:34: Native Vulgate Numbers 10:34-36 place the cloud notice first (10:34), followed by the lifting up (10:35) and setting down (10:36) of the ark, matching the Hebrew order (mapping to Saints.Bible Septuagint-aligned order 10:36, 10:34, 10:35).
notes.10:35: In the Clementine Vulgate, verses 10:34-36 stand in a different order from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Vulgate 10:34-35 correspond to MT 10:35-36, and Vulgate 10:36 corresponds to MT 10:34); in 10:35 the Vulgate also reads "multitude of the army of Israel" where the Hebrew has "ten thousands of the thousands of Israel."
notes.11:3: Latin Incensio ("Burning") translates the meaning of the Hebrew place name Taberah rather than transliterating it.
notes.11:15: Vulgate Sin aliter tibi videtur ("But if it seems otherwise to You") and the coordinated clause et inveniam gratiam ("and that I may find favor") diverge from the Hebrew, which reads "If this is how you are going to treat me... if I have found favor in your sight."
notes.11:25: Vulgate nec ultra cessaverunt ("and did not cease anymore") conveys the opposite sense of the Hebrew ve-lo yasafu, normally understood as "and they did not do so again."
notes.11:28: Vulgate electus e pluribus ("chosen from among many") reflects the Hebrew root "to choose," whereas the Masoretic vocalization means "from his youth."
notes.11:34: Latin Sepulchra concupiscentiae ("Graves of Craving") translates the Hebrew place name Kibroth-hattaavah; the Clementine Vulgate also combines Masoretic Text 11:34 and 11:35 into a single verse, giving chapter 11 thirty-four verses.
notes.12:1: The Vulgate reads 'Aethiopissam' ("Ethiopian woman"), matching the Septuagint, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Cushite woman."
notes.12:4: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "tent of meeting" as 'tabernaculum foederis' ("tabernacle of the covenant") and adds 'tantum' ("alone") to "the three of you."
notes.12:6: The Vulgate explicitly reads 'propheta Domini' ("a prophet of the Lord"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "your prophet" (or "a prophet among you") without "of the Lord" in this clause.
notes.12:8: In a Vulgate-distinct construction, 'et figuras' ("and figures") is governed by 'non per' ("not through") while 'Dominum' ("the Lord") is the direct object of 'videt' ("he sees"), whereas the Hebrew reads that Moses beholds "the form of the Lord."
notes.13:1: Native Vulgate Numbers 13:1 maps to Saints.Bible 12:16, and native 13:2-34 map to Saints.Bible 13:1-33.
notes.13:12: Where the Hebrew repeats 'matteh' ("staff/tribe"), the Vulgate renders the second occurrence literally as 'sceptri' ("of the scepter") alongside 'tribu' ("tribe").
notes.13:23: The Vulgate uses the Greco-Latin name 'Tanim' (Tanis), matching the Septuagint, for the Egyptian city called Zoan in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.13:25: The Vulgate transliterates the Hebrew place name 'Nahal Eshcol' as a single name 'Nehelescol' and supplies the explanatory gloss 'id est Torrens botri' ("that is, the Stream of the Cluster").
notes.13:31: The Vulgate expands the Hebrew ("Caleb quieted the people before Moses") by explicitly naming 'murmur populi, qui oriebatur contra Moysen' ("the murmuring of the people, who were rising up against Moses").
notes.13:34: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew 'Nephilim' as 'monstra quaedam ... de genere giganteo' ("certain monsters ... of the giant race") and omits the Masoretic Text's final clause ("in our own sight, and so we were in their sight"), ending with 'quasi locustae videbamur' ("we seemed like locusts").
notes.14:3: The Vulgate adds "vast" (vasta) to the wilderness, shifts to a present-tense wish ("if only we might perish," utinam pereamus), and continues with a negative wish ("may the Lord not lead us") rather than the Hebrew question ("Why is the Lord bringing us?").
notes.14:10: Latin super tectum foederis literally reads "above the roof of the covenant," a distinctive Vulgate wording for the covering of the tent of meeting.
notes.14:12: Latin faciam principem super gentem magnam specifies making Moses a ruler over a great nation, whereas the Hebrew reads making him into a greater and mightier nation.
notes.14:18: Latin nullumque innoxium derelinquens literally means "leaving no one guiltless" (or "unpunished"), rendering the objectless Hebrew idiom for not acquitting guilt. The verb visitas ("You who visit") shifts into second-person address within the quoted proclamation.
notes.14:44: Latin contenebrati ("darkened," i.e., blinded in mind) is a distinctive Vulgate rendering reflecting a connection between the Hebrew verb for acting presumptuously and the Hebrew root for darkness.
notes.15:5: The Clementine Vulgate attaches "For individual lambs" (Per agnos singulos, closing 15:5) to "and rams" (et arietes, opening 15:6) under the two-tenths flour and third-of-a-hin measure, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text closes the preceding one-tenth/fourth-of-a-hin measure with "for each lamb."
notes.15:11: Native Vulgate Numbers 15:11-18 divide the clauses previously merged into 15:11 under the Greek-slotted anchor (native 15:11 'Sic facies', 15:12 'per singulos boves...', 15:13-18 continuing the law of offerings).
notes.15:20: Latin de cibis vestris ("from your foods") here and de pulmentis ("from the cooked dishes") in 15:21 are distinctly Vulgate renderings of the rare Hebrew term usually understood as coarse meal or dough.
notes.15:25: Latin incensum ("incense") here renders the Hebrew term for a fire-offering, and the Vulgate adds pro se ("for themselves") alongside "for their sin and error."
notes.15:30: Latin per superbiam ("through pride") renders the Hebrew idiom "with a high hand" (meaning defiant, deliberate sin), and rebellis fuit ("has been rebellious") stands where the Hebrew reads "blasphemes."
notes.16:1: The Vulgate introduces the rebellion with Ecce autem ("Now look") and joins Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and On directly to "rose up" (surrexerunt) in 16:2, smoothing a difficult Hebrew verb ("took") that lacks an explicit object.
notes.16:9: Latin singular ei ("to Him") is grammatically ambiguous: it naturally parallels the preceding serviretis ei ("serve Him," referring to God), though it can also refer to frequentia ("the throng," corresponding to Hebrew plural "them").
notes.16:14: Unlike the Hebrew negative ("you have not brought us"), the Vulgate has the affirmative Revera induxisti nos ("Indeed, you have brought us") and reads "our eyes" (oculos nostros) rather than "the eyes of these men."
notes.16:30: Latin in infernum ("into the underworld") is the Vulgate's standard term for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol), and blasphemaverint ("have blasphemed") renders Hebrew "have despised/spurned."
notes.16:35: In this versification, as in the Hebrew, Numbers 16 ends at 16:35, and the subsequent account of the bronze censers begins Numbers 17.
notes.16:38: The Vulgate reads "in the deaths of the sinners" (Latin "in mortibus peccatorum"), whereas the Hebrew reads "at the cost of their lives."
notes.16:42: In native Clementine Vulgate numbering, 16:36-50 conclude chapter 16 (mapped to Saints.Bible 17:1-15).
notes.16:47: The Vulgate uses "incendium" ("blaze" or "fire") for what was devastating the multitude, matching 17:2 and 17:4, whereas the Hebrew refers here to "the plague."
notes.17:1: Native Vulgate Numbers 16:36-50 contain the censers and plague (Saints.Bible 17:1-15), and native Numbers 17:1-13 contain Aaron's budding rod (Saints.Bible 17:16-28).
notes.17:6: The Vulgate specifies "apart from the rod of Aaron" (Latin "absque virga Aaron"), indicating twelve tribal rods in addition to Aaron's, whereas the Hebrew places Aaron's staff "among their staffs."
notes.18:2: "Scepter of your father" translates Latin "sceptrum patris tui," rendering Hebrew "shevet" in its sense of "rod" or "scepter" rather than "tribe."
notes.18:8: Throughout Chapter 18 (18:8, 11, 19, 26, 28, 30), the Vulgate translates the Hebrew term for "contribution" or "heave offering" ("terumah") as "primitiae" ("firstfruits").
notes.18:12: "Marrow" translates Latin "medullam," a literal Vulgate idiom for the richest or choicest part of the oil, wine, and grain (corresponding to Hebrew "fat").
notes.18:16: "Obols" translates Latin "obolos," a Greco-Roman unit of weight used in the Vulgate (following the Septuagint) in place of the Hebrew "gerah."
notes.18:32: Unlike the Hebrew (which states that the Levites will incur no sin once they contribute the best part), the Vulgate frames this verse as a prohibition against reserving the choice and fat portions for themselves ("egregia vobis et pinguia reservantes").
notes.19:2: Latin religio victimae ("rite of the sacrifice") corresponds to Hebrew "statute of the law," and aetatis integrae ("of full age," literally "of unimpaired age") renders Hebrew temimah ("unblemished") alongside in qua nulla sit macula ("in which there is no blemish").
notes.19:3: The Vulgate has Eleazar himself sacrifice the cow in conspectu omnium ("in the sight of all") and burn her cunctis videntibus ("while all look on," v. 5), whereas the Hebrew text has another person slaughter and burn her in Eleazar's presence.
notes.19:18: The Vulgate summarizes the Hebrew list of corpse-defilement sources with the concise phrase homines hujuscemodi contagione pollutos ("the people defiled by a contagion of this kind").
notes.19:19: The Vulgate reads immundus erit usque ad vesperum ("he will be unclean until evening"), as in verses 8, 10, 21, and 22, whereas the Hebrew states that he will be "clean at evening."
notes.20:6: The prayer of Moses and Aaron ("and they cried out to the Lord and said ... their murmuring may cease") is a notable Vulgate-distinct addition not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text or the Septuagint.
notes.20:13: Latin aqua contradictionis ("water of contradiction," and plural aquas contradictionis in v. 24) translates the Hebrew place-name Meribah ("contention/strife") rather than transliterating it.
notes.20:17: Latin via publica ("the public road") renders Hebrew "the king's highway" in Roman idiom; likewise in v. 19 the Vulgate renders Hebrew's brief idiom ("only let me pass on foot") as "there will be no difficulty over the price; only let us pass through quickly."
notes.20:24: Latin eo quod incredulus fuerit ori meo ("because he was unbelieving toward My mouth," preserving the Hebraism "mouth" for spoken command) uses third-person singular for Aaron where Hebrew has second-person plural ("because you rebelled against My word"), echoing rebelles et increduli ("rebels and unbelievers") in v. 10.
notes.20:28: Native Vulgate Numbers 20 divides Aaron's death and mourning across 20:28-30 (mapping to Saints.Bible 20:28-29), ending with per cunctas familias suas ("throughout all its families") where the Hebrew has "all the house of Israel."
notes.20:30: Native Clementine Vulgate divides Aaron's death across 20:28-30 (mapped to Saints.Bible 20:28-29), ending with per cunctas familias suas ("throughout all its families") where the Hebrew has "all the house of Israel."
notes.21:1: The Vulgate renders Hebrew derek ha-atarim (often taken as a place name, 'the way of Atharim') as a descriptive phrase, exploratorum viam ('the way of the scouts').
notes.21:3: The Vulgate adds the explanatory gloss id est, anathema ('that is, anathema', referring to something placed under the ban or devoted to destruction) to clarify the name Hormah, a gloss not present in the Hebrew text.
notes.21:14: Where the Hebrew text contains the obscure phrase 'Waheb in Suphah and the wadis of Arnon,' the Vulgate understands Suphah as 'the Red Sea' (mari Rubro) and supplies a complete parallel comparison.
notes.21:18: The Vulgate translates Hebrew bimchoqeq personally as in datore legis ('with the giver of the law') rather than instrumentally as 'with the scepter' or 'commander's staff.'
notes.21:30: The Vulgate reflects a distinct interpretation of this difficult Hebrew verse, rendering niram as jugum ipsorum ('their yoke') and wannashim as lassi ('weary'); the Clementine Latin text also reads ad Hesebon ('at Heshbon') rather than 'from Heshbon.'
notes.22:5: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew place-name Pethor as a common noun, "a diviner" (ariolum), and reads "the sons of Ammon" (filiorum Ammon) where the Masoretic Text has "the sons of his people."
notes.22:9: The Vulgate asks "What do these men with you want?" (Quid sibi volunt), whereas the Hebrew text asks "Who are these men with you?"
notes.22:22: The Vulgate simply states "And God became angry" (Et iratus est Deus), omitting the Hebrew causal clause "because he was going."
notes.22:39: Where the Hebrew text gives the place-name Kiriath-huzoth, the Vulgate translates it descriptively as "a city that was on the farthest borders of his kingdom."
notes.23:4: The Vulgate reads "quickly" (velociter) where the Hebrew text has "to a bare height" (shephi).
notes.23:7: Latin "parable" (parabola, also in 23:18) reflects the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew mashal, here referring to a poetic prophetic oracle or discourse.
notes.23:14: The Vulgate reads "a high place" (locum sublimem) instead of the Hebrew "field of Zophim," and explicitly names Balaam as the builder of the seven altars rather than leaving the subject as Balak.
notes.23:21: The Vulgate distinctively reads "idol" (idolum) and "image" (simulacrum) where the Hebrew has "iniquity" and "trouble," and adds "of victory" (victoriae) to "the king."
notes.23:22: The Vulgate renders Hebrew re'em ("wild ox") as "rhinoceros" (rhinocerotis), a distinctive Latin reading also found in Numbers 24:8 and Job 39:9.
notes.24:3: Vulgate cujus obturatus est oculus ("whose eye is closed") renders the debated Hebrew term as "closed," creating a deliberate contrast with "and thus his eyes are opened" in 24:4.
notes.24:7: Vulgate Tolletur propter Agag, rex ejus, et auferetur regnum illius ("His king will be removed because of Agag, and his kingdom will be taken away") differs from the Hebrew ("his king will be higher than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted").
notes.24:8: Vulgate rhinocerotis ("rhinoceros") renders Hebrew re'em ("wild ox"; Septuagint "unicorn").
notes.24:14: Vulgate quid populus tuus populo huic faciat ("what your people will do to this people") reverses the subject and object of the Hebrew ("what this people will do to your people").
notes.24:22: Vulgate et fueris electus de stirpe Cin ("and have been chosen from the lineage of Kain") differs markedly from the Hebrew ("yet Kain will be consumed").
notes.24:24: The Vulgate renders Hebrew Kittim as Italia ("Italy"), specifies in trieribus ("in triremes"), and translates Hebrew Eber as Hebraeos ("the Hebrews").
notes.25:3: Vulgate Initiatusque est ("was initiated into," also in 25:5) follows the Septuagint in describing Israel's attachment to Baal-peor in terms of cultic initiation (Hebrew: "yoked/joined itself to").
notes.25:4: Vulgate in patibulis ("on gallows") specifies the instrument of public execution and does not include the Hebrew phrase "to the Lord."
notes.25:8: The Vulgate distinctively reads scortum ("prostitute") in 25:6, pugione ("dagger") in 25:7, and lupanar ("brothel") with in locis genitalibus ("in the genital parts") here, where the Hebrew refers to a Midianite woman, a spear, an inner chamber, and her belly.
notes.25:12: Vulgate pacem foederis mei ("the peace of My covenant") inverts the Hebrew genitive construction ("My covenant of peace").
notes.26:1: The Vulgate reads 'After the blood of the guilty had been poured out' (Postquam noxiorum sanguis effusus est), referring back to the executions in chapter 25, whereas the Masoretic Text reads 'After the plague.'
notes.26:3: In verses 3-4, the Vulgate has Moses and Eleazar speak directly to those twenty years old and above without quoting a census command or mentioning the departure from Egypt, transitioning straight to 'and this is their number.'
notes.26:10: The Vulgate reads 'devoured Korah while very many died' and links verses 10-11 into a single statement ('And a great miracle took place, that while Korah perished, his sons did not perish'), whereas the Masoretic Text says the earth swallowed them along with Korah so they became a warning sign, before separately stating that Korah's sons did not die.
notes.26:15: Native Vulgate Numbers 26:15-47 follow the Hebrew/Vulgate tribal sequence (Gad 26:15-18, Judah 26:19-22, Issachar 26:23-25, Zebulun 26:26-27, Manasseh 26:28-34, Ephraim 26:35-37, Benjamin 26:38-41, Dan 26:42-43, Asher 26:44-47), differing from Saints.Bible Septuagint-aligned order.
notes.26:17: The Vulgate names Gad's seventh son 'Ariel' (with the 'Arielites') and his fifth son 'Her' ('Er' in v. 25, matching Judah's son in v. 15), whereas the Masoretic Text has 'Areli' ('Arelites') and 'Eri'; likewise, Latin 'Selaitarum' (v. 16, 'Shelahites') and 'Phuaitarum' (v. 19, 'Puahites') lack the '-n-' of Hebrew 'Shelanites' and 'Punites.'
notes.26:19: From verse 15 through verse 31, the Clementine Vulgate orders the tribes as Judah (vv. 15-18), Issachar (vv. 19-21), Zebulun (vv. 22-23), Gad (vv. 24-27), and Asher (vv. 28-31), resulting in a different tribal sequence and verse numbering from the Masoretic Text.
notes.26:39: The Vulgate reads 'Supham' ('Shupham') rather than the Masoretic Text's longer form 'Shephupham,' and in verse 44 reads 'Noemanitarum' ('Naamanites'), retaining the '-n-' where the Masoretic Text has 'Naamites.'
notes.26:43: The Vulgate reads 'All were Shuhamites' (Omnes fuere Suhamitae), whereas the Masoretic Text reads 'All the families of the Shuhamites according to those numbered of them.'
notes.26:55: In verses 55-56, the Vulgate specifies that the lot divides the land among the tribes and families and directs that both the more numerous and the fewer must accept whatever falls by lot, differing in structure from the Masoretic Text's statement that the inheritance is divided by lot between the larger and the smaller.
notes.26:58: Unlike the '-itarum' clan endings used in verse 57, the Vulgate lists these five Levite divisions as 'familia Lobni, familia Hebroni, familia Moholi, familia Musi, familia Core,' rendered here with the ancestor names Libni, Hebron, Mahli, Mushi, and Korah.
notes.27:2: Latin "tabernaculi foederis" ("tabernacle of the covenant") is the Vulgate's characteristic rendering of the Hebrew "tent of meeting."
notes.27:3: Native Clementine Vulgate divides the daughters of Zelophehad episode across 27:3-8; distinctive Vulgate readings include "in the rebellion that was stirred up... under Korah," "the relatives of our father," and "to the judgment of the Lord" (v. 4). Native Vulgate Numbers 27:3-8 divide Zelophehad's daughters' petition and the Lord's ruling into separate verses 27:3-8 (fixing the old merged 27:3). Notice the Vulgate's distinctive renderings "in the rebellion that was stirred up... under Korah," "the relatives of our father," and "to the judgment of the Lord."
notes.27:14: Latin "Sin" renders Hebrew Zin (just as "Sion" renders Zion), and "aquae contradictionis" ("waters of Contention," literally "contradiction") translates the Hebrew place name Meribah.
notes.27:21: The Vulgate states simply that Eleazar will consult the Lord "if anything is to be done," omitting the Hebrew reference to the judgment of the Urim.
notes.27:23: Latin "capiti ejus" ("on his head") specifies where Moses laid his hands, and "replicavit" ("repeated") differs from the Hebrew "commissioned him."
notes.28:2: Latin "incensum" (literally "that which is burned/kindled," often "incense") is used throughout this chapter (vv. 2, 6, 13, 19) for the sacrificial fire offering.
notes.28:6: Vulgate "quod obtulistis" ("that you offered") is active second-person plural, differing from the Hebrew passive participle ("which was ordained"); similarly in v. 7, Vulgate "vini" ("wine") renders Hebrew "strong drink."
notes.28:10: The Vulgate links this verse directly to the drink offerings ("which are duly poured out... as a perpetual burnt offering," and similarly v. 15), whereas the Hebrew places these offerings "besides" the continual burnt offering.
notes.28:13: Latin "decimam decimae" (literally "a tenth of a tenth," also in vv. 21 and 29) renders the Hebrew distributive repetition "a tenth [of an ephah] each" as a nested fraction.
notes.28:24: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "food of the fire offering" as "fuel for the fire" ("in fomitem ignis") and explicitly describes the sweet fragrance as rising from the burnt offering and each offering's libations.
notes.28:29: Native Vulgate Numbers 28:29-31 divide these offerings across separate verses 28:29-31 (fixing the old merged 28:29), and render Hebrew "its grain offering" as "its drink offerings" ("liba ejus").
notes.28:30: Native Clementine Vulgate divides this passage across 28:29-31, and renders Hebrew "its grain offering" as "its drink offerings" ("liba ejus").
notes.29:1: Vulgate 'venerabilis et sancta' ("venerable and holy"; also in vv. 7, 12) translates Hebrew miqra qodesh ("holy convocation").
notes.29:6: Vulgate 'calendarum' uses the Roman term for the first day of the month, corresponding to Hebrew hachodesh ("the new moon"); 'incensum' literally denotes a burned or fire offering (Hebrew isheh).
notes.29:10: Vulgate 'decimam decimae' ("a tenth of a tenth"; also in v. 15) renders the Hebrew distributive idiom issaron issaron ("a tenth each") as a genitive phrase; contrast 'unam decimam' ("one tenth") in v. 4.
notes.29:14: Vulgate reads 'in libamentis eorum' ("in their libations") here instead of 'in sacrificiis eorum' ("in their sacrifices") as in vv. 3 and 9, and adds the explanatory gloss 'id est, simul arietibus duobus' ("that is, for the two rams together").
notes.29:35: Vulgate 'qui est celeberrimus' ("which is most celebrated") translates Hebrew atseret ("a solemn assembly").
notes.30:1: As in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, chapter 30 begins with this verse; in the alternative versification it is numbered 29:40, and verses 30:2-17 here are numbered 30:1-16.
notes.30:4: The classical Latin legal idiom 'voti rea' (also in v. 8; compare 'promissionis rea' in v. 13) means bound by or liable for a vow, rather than morally guilty.
notes.30:7: Vulgate 'semel de ore ejus verbum egrediens' ("a word once going forth from her mouth") corresponds to Hebrew mivta sefateiha ("the rash utterance of her lips").
notes.30:14: Vulgate adds the explanatory phrase 'per jejunium, vel ceterarum rerum abstinentiam' ("through fasting or abstinence from other things"), which is absent from the Hebrew text, and renders the husband's authority to confirm or annul the vow as 'in arbitrio viri erit ut faciat, sive non faciat'.
notes.30:17: Vulgate 'vel quae manet in parentis domo' ("or who remains in her parent's house") introduces an alternative clause ('vel') and uses gender-neutral 'parentis' ("parent's"), where the Hebrew has a single phrase ("in her youth in her father's house").
notes.31:7: The Vulgate adds atque vicissent ("and were victorious") and omits the Hebrew clause "as the Lord commanded Moses."
notes.31:14: The Vulgate renders the Israelite officers of thousands and hundreds with the Roman military titles tribunis ("tribunes") and centurionibus ("centurions"), which also recur in vv. 48 and 52.
notes.31:29: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew tribute/contribution (terumah) as primitiae ("firstfruits"), a distinctive choice repeated in v. 41.
notes.31:42: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which begins the congregation's half here, the Vulgate joins v. 42 to v. 41 with the dative his ("for those who had been in the battle"), then contrasts it with the remaining multitude's half in v. 43 (De media vero parte).
notes.31:50: The Vulgate translates the final two golden ornaments as dextralia ("bracelets" for the right arm or wrist) and muraenulas ("chain necklaces"), and renders the closing purpose clause as a request for Moses's intercession (ut depreceris pro nobis Dominum, "so that you may pray to the Lord for us") rather than Hebrew "to make atonement for our souls before the Lord."
notes.32:9: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Eshcol ("cluster") literally into Latin as Vallem botri ("the Valley of the Cluster").
notes.32:11: Latin Si videbunt (literally "If they will see") preserves the Hebraic negative oath idiom meaning "Surely they will not see."
notes.32:14: The Vulgate inserts inquit ("he said") to mark Moses resuming direct address after recounting the Lord's oath, and renders Hebrew "brood" with the doubled phrase incrementa et alumni ("offspring and nurslings").
notes.32:35: The Vulgate (et Etroth, et Sophan) divides the single Hebrew compound place name Atroth-shophan into two separate towns.
notes.32:41: The Vulgate adds the explanatory gloss id est, Villas Jair ("that is, the Villages of Jair") to translate the Hebrew place name Havvoth-jair.
notes.33:2: The Vulgate omits the Hebrew's repeated second clause and links "at the command of the Lord" directly to the Israelites' changing of their camp sites (quae Domini jussione mutabant).
notes.33:16: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Kibroth-hattaavah into Latin as sepulchra concupiscentiae ("the Graves of Craving"; cf. Numbers 11:34).
notes.33:32: The Vulgate reads montem Gadgad ("Mount Gadgad"), interpreting the first element of the Hebrew place name Hor-haggidgad as "mount" (hor).
notes.33:40: With the accusative in terram Chanaan ("into the land of Canaan"), the Vulgate construes the phrase as the destination of Israel's arrival rather than as part of the description of where the king of Arad lived (as in the Hebrew).
notes.33:52: In verses 52-55, the Vulgate intensifies the Hebrew commands to "drive out" and "dispossess" into disperdite ("destroy"), mundantes terram ("cleansing the land," v. 53), and interficere ("kill," v. 55), and renders the Hebrew "figured stones" as titulos ("monuments").
notes.34:4: The Vulgate translates Hebrew Akrabbim as singular Latin Scorpionis ("of the Scorpion"), renders Hebrew Tsinah as Senna (distinct from Sin/Zin in v. 3, following the Septuagint), and translates the first element of Hazar-addar as villam nomine Adar ("the village named Addar").
notes.34:7: Where the Hebrew reads "Mount Hor" (Hor ha-har), the Vulgate translates descriptively as montem altissimum ("the highest mountain").
notes.34:11: The Vulgate reads contra fontem Daphnim ("opposite the spring Daphnis"), naming the spring where the Hebrew has only Ain ("spring").
notes.34:26: The Vulgate includes the title dux ("leader") only for Issachar's representative in this list, whereas the Hebrew applies the title nasi to each of the last seven tribal chiefs.
notes.35:4: The Vulgate gives mille passuum spatio ("a distance of a thousand paces," a Roman mile) where the Hebrew has "a thousand cubits," though the Vulgate retains "two thousand cubits" in v. 5.
notes.35:22: The Vulgate condenses vv. 22-25 into one sentence across native 35:22-25, without the specific examples of accidental killing given in Hebrew vv. 22-23. Native Vulgate Numbers 35:22-25 divide the condensed accidental-killing law across four verses (35:22 'But if by chance and without hatred', 35:23 'and hostilities he has done any of these things', 35:24-25), without the specific examples of accidental killing given in Hebrew 35:22-23.
notes.35:24: Latin propinquum sanguinis ("close relative of the blood") renders Hebrew go'el ha-dam ("avenger of blood," translated ultor sanguinis in v. 27).
notes.35:32: Unlike the Hebrew, which forbids accepting a ransom to let a fugitive return early, the Vulgate states directly that exiles and fugitives may by no means return before the high priest's death.
notes.35:33: The Vulgate specifies insontium cruore ("the blood of the innocent") where the Hebrew says simply "blood," and in v. 34 turns the prohibition against defiling the land into the promise emundabitur vestra possessio ("your possession will be cleansed").
notes.36:4: The Vulgate adds the explanatory gloss id est, quinquagesimus annus remissionis ("that is, the fiftieth year of release") and summarizes the consequence as confusion of the lots and transfer of possessions among tribes.
notes.36:8: The Vulgate generalizes the marriage requirement to all men (36:7) and all women (36:8) rather than only to inheriting daughters as in the Hebrew.
